extracted.intended_audience: students, educators, and the general public interested in how scientific peer review and publication work
extracted.subtask_description: Explains the peer review process and the standards used to judge whether a scientific article is suitable for publication, including procedural steps (submission → review → revision) and substantive quality criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting by experts in the relevant field
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal’s editors send the article to several other scientists who work in the same field (i.e., the “peers” of peer review). Those reviewers provide feedback on the article and tell the editor whether or not they think the study is of high enough quality to be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer reviewers are domain experts who evaluate the work and advise the editor; their assessment is a primary basis for publication decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledges and builds upon other work in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Only articles that meet good scientific standards (e.g., acknowledge and build upon other work in the field ...) are accepted for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should situate their work within existing literature, citing relevant prior studies and showing how the new work extends or revises that body of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relies on logical reasoning and well-designed studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Only articles that meet good scientific standards (e.g., ... rely on logical reasoning and well-designed studies ...) are accepted for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators look for sound argumentation and study designs appropriate to the question (controls, sample size, methods, analysis) that support valid inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backs up claims with evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Only articles that meet good scientific standards (e.g., ... back up claims with evidence ...) are accepted for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions must be supported by data or other verifiable evidence; unjustified assertions are a reason for rejection or revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision and resubmission after reviewer feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors may then revise their article and resubmit it for consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review is iterative: authors are expected to respond to reviewer critiques and improve the manuscript before acceptance; this is part of meeting the field's standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meets minimum standards for scientific quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review helps provide assurance that published research meets minimum standards for scientific quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication indicates the work has passed community thresholds for methodology, reasoning, and evidence, even though it may not be definitive or error-free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review indicates community standards met, not guaranteed correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-reviewed work isn’t necessarily correct or conclusive, but it does meet the standards of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should understand that acceptance means conformity with current scientific standards; subsequent work may confirm, extend, or overturn published findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability and community response as part of quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a piece of scientific research passes through peer review and is published, science must deal with it somehow — perhaps by incorporating it into the established body of scientific knowledge, building on it further, figuring out why it is wrong, or trying to replicate its results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replication, follow-up studies, and incorporation into later work are mechanisms by which the community further evaluates and solidifies (or rejects) published findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review is time-consuming and competitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review and publication are time-consuming, frequently involving more than a year between submission and publication. The process is also highly competitive (example acceptance rates cited: Science <8%, NEJM ~6%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High selectivity and lengthy review timelines mean publication is a gatekeeping process; low acceptance rates reflect stringent quality thresholds but also competitive constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review as a general quality-assurance mechanism across fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Many fields outside of science use peer review to ensure quality (e.g., philosophy journals, figure-skating judging panels, wine competitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While described in a scientific context here, the core principle—evaluation by knowledgeable peers—is a broadly used standard for assessing quality in diverse domains.
